old: Radioactive decay is exponential, so the time is not simply proportional to the fraction decayed.
new: This multiplies the half-life by the lead-to-uranium ratio, 4/16. Decay is exponential, so use ln(N₀/N) = kt with N₀ = 20 and N = 16.
why: 1.12e9 = 0.25 × 4.47e9; a truly linear model would give 1.79e9, so 'not proportional to fraction decayed' misdescribes the error

old: The box has 16 U and 4 Pb atoms, so the crystal began with 20 U atoms and 16/20 = 0.800 remain. k = 0.693/(4.47×109 yr) = 1.55×10−10 yr−1; t = ln(20/16)/k = 0.223/1.55×10−10 = 1.44×109 yr (1.439e+9). 1.86×109 yr takes 75% (12 of 16) as the fraction left, 1.12×109 yr treats decay as linear, and 8.94×109 yr is two half-lives.
new: The box has 16 U and 4 Pb atoms, so the crystal began with 20 U atoms and 16/20 = 0.800 remain. k = 0.693/(4.47×109 yr) = 1.55×10−10 yr−1; t = ln(20/16)/k = 0.223/1.55×10−10 = 1.44×109 yr. 1.86×109 yr takes 75% (12 of 16) as the fraction left, 1.12×109 yr multiplies the half-life by the Pb : U ratio (4/16), and 8.94×109 yr is two half-lives.
